column2: He gives breaths and splendour to beings, bull of the Bharatas, who quickly gives food to a seeker who has come to his house.
[Bhishma said:] Thus told by Narada, I always gave food, king; you too, free of envy, give food; therefore give it without fever.
Having duly given food to brahmanas, king, lord, suitably worthy, you too will then gain heaven.
Hear, lord of men, the worlds of givers of food: in heaven the dwellings of those great souls shine, of various shapes and forms, with various pillars,
white like the moon's disc, with nets of little bells, the colour of the young sun, standing and moving,
with many hundreds of floors, with water and groves inside, shining like beryl and sun, made of silver and gold,
with trees bearing fruits of all desires standing at the houses, with ponds, lanes, halls, wells and long lakes on all sides,
with sounding vehicles harnessed by the thousand, mountains made of food and drink, garments and ornaments,
rivers flowing with milk, mountains of grain, palaces pale like clouds, and beds bright with gold; givers of food reach those; therefore be a giver of food.
These are the worlds of the great-souled givers of food who do good deeds; therefore food should be especially given by men on earth.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Devaki and the divine sage Narada.
To Narada, of divine sight, who had come to Dvaraka, Devaki, seer of dharma, then put a question.
As she asked, the divine sage Narada told everything duly; hear that, lord of men.
[Narada said:] "Greatly fortunate one, one who satisfies brahmanas and the good with pudding and ghee under the Krittikas gains unsurpassed worlds.
Under Rohini, famed meats, beans, grain and ghee, with milk to drink after, should be given to a twice-born for freedom from debt.
Giving a milch cow with calf under the star whose deity is Soma, they go from the world of men to unsurpassed heaven.
Giving krisara mixed with oil under Ardra and fasting, a man crosses hard places and mountains with razor-edged ridges.
Giving cakes under Punarvasu and likewise grain under the auspicious one, he is born in a family with much food, glorious and handsome.
Giving sesame-filled and growing things under the Maghas, a man rejoices here and hereafter with sons and cattle.
Fasting before Phalguni, giving foods with molasses to brahmanas, he attains good fortune.
Giving duly shashtika rice with ghee and milk under Uttara, he is honoured in heaven.
Whatever gift is given by men under Uttara, it is certain that it has great and endless fruit.
Giving an elephant-chariot yoked with four under Hasta while fasting, he gains the highest worlds joined with desires of merit.
Giving a bull and holy scents under Chitra, Bharata, he moves in the world of apsarases and delights in Nandana.
Giving wealth, whatever is dearest to him, under Svati, he gains good worlds and great fame here.
Under Vishakha, giving an ox and a milch cow, and a cart with its loads, with grain and clothing,
he pleases ancestors and gods and gains endlessness after death; he does not meet hard places and goes to heaven.
Having given to brahmanas as told, he finds the wished livelihood and does not meet hell and other afflictions: so it is certain.
Giving a covering garment under Anuradha, fasting, and a hundred yokes also, a man is honoured in heaven.
Giving kalashaka with radish to brahmins under Jyeshtha, a mortal gains the wished prosperity and the wished goal.
Giving root and fruit to brahmanas under Mula, composed, he pleases the ancestors and goes to the wished goal.
Then fasting under Purvashadha and giving curd vessels to a brahmana of family conduct, a master of the Vedas, he is born after death in a family with many cattle.
Giving udamantha with ghee, abundant honey and molasses under Uttarashadha, he would gain all desires.
Giving milk joined with honey and ghee at the conjunction of Abhijit to the wise, constant in dharma, he is honoured in heaven.
Giving a blanket covered with a garment under Shravana, he goes with a white vehicle to all unobstructed worlds.
Giving, composed, a vehicle yoked with cows, with reins of cloth, under Dhanishtha, he at once gains a kingdom after death.
Giving scents, aloe and sandal at the conjunction of Shatabhishak, he gains the worlds of apsarases and eternal scents after death.
Giving rajamasha under Purvabhadrapada, joined with fruit of all foods, he becomes happy after death.
He who gives ram's meat at the conjunction of Uttara pleases the ancestors and gains endlessness after death.
He who gives a cow with a bronze milk-pail under Revati: she, after death, takes desires and attends the giver.
The best of men who gives a chariot yoked with horses under Ashvini is born in a family rich in elephants, horses and chariots, splendid.
Giving a sesame cow to the twice-born under Bharani, a man gains many cows and fame after death."
[Bhishma said:] Thus this indication according to the conjunction of the stars was told here by Narada to Devaki, and she told it to her daughters-in-law.
Holy, pure, life-giving and imperishable for the ancestors is gold, as declared by the king Harishchandra.
Manu said giving drinking water is the highest of gifts; therefore one should dig ponds, wells and tanks.
A well with water flowing, well-set going always, removes half the sin of a man's deed here.
He carries his whole line across in whose dug reservoir cows, brahmanas, and good men always drink.
He whose water stands unobstructed in the hot season never meets hard places, rough and difficult.
The blessed Brihaspati, Pushan, Bhaga, the Ashvins and Agni are pleased with ghee.
It is the highest medicine, the best of sacrifices, the best of juices and the best of fruits.
A man wishing fruit, fame and nourishment should always give ghee to the twice-born, pure and self-possessed.
His aims and various works always succeed, and he shines in body above his enemies.
The blessed Agni is always very pleased with him; animals do not leave him, and he wins in battle.
One who gives an umbrella gains sons and prosperity; he does not get eye disease, and he enjoys a share of sacrifice.
One who gives an umbrella in the hot season or rains never gets any burning of mind, and from hardship and rough ground he gains release, brahmana.
The gift of a cart is distinguished among all gifts; so said the greatly fortunate blessed sage Shandilya.
[Bhishma said:] One who gives sandals to brahmanas, composed, treads all thorns and crosses rough places, and stands above his enemies, Yudhishthira.
A lovely vehicle yoked with mules, adorned with silver and gold, waits on him, Kaunteya; and a cart yoked with young oxen is given.
[Yudhishthira said:] The fruit told of the gift of sesame and of land, tell me more of cows and of food, Kauravya.
[Bhishma said:] Hear from me, Kaunteya, the fruit of giving sesame, and having heard, give duly, best of the Kurus.
Sesame was created by the Self-born as the first food of the ancestors; therefore by the gift of sesame the fortnight of the ancestors rejoices.
He who gives sesame to brahmanas in the month of Magha does not see a hell crowded with all beings.
One who sacrifices to ancestors with sesame sacrifices with all desires; a sesame funeral rite should never be given without desire.
These sesame came forth from the limbs of the great sage Kashyapa; thence sesame went to a divine state in gifts, lord.
The gods, assembling before Brahma, wishing to sacrifice, asked for a lovely place of earth, king: "Let us sacrifice."

[The gods said:] "Blessed one, you are lord of the whole earth and heaven; we would sacrifice with your permission, greatly fortunate one; for without permission the earth does not yield the fruit of sacrifice.
You are lord of the whole world, moving and unmoving; therefore you ought to permit."
[Brahma said:] "I give you, best of gods, a portion of earth; in whatever place you do the sacrifice, sons of Kashyapa."
[The gods said:] "Blessed one, our desires fulfilled, we shall sacrifice with proper fees; but sages always frequent this place."
[Bhishma said:] Then Agastya, Kanva, Bhrigu, Atri, Vrisha, Kapi, Asita and Devala came to the gods' sacrifice.
Then the great-souled gods, unfallen one, performed the sacrifice, and the best of gods completed it in due time.
Those gods, having performed the sacrifice on the Himalaya, best of mountains, made a gift of land of a sixth part of the sacrifice.
One who gives even a span of land, unadorned, does not sink in hardships nor meet hard places.
Giving a well-prepared house-ground that endures cold, wind and heat, he stays in the world of the gods and is not shaken even at the end of his merit.
The wise one lives glad with Shakra, lord of earth; and the giver of a pleasure-shelter is honoured in heaven.
A Shrotriya of controlled senses, born in a family of teachers, who lives satisfied in whose house, gains the chief world.
So too a great shelter for cows, bearing cold and rain, carries the family across to the seventh generation, best of the Bharatas.
Giving field land in the world, one would gain sons and prosperity; giving jewel-land, one would increase the family line.
One should never give salty or burnt land, nor land surrounded by cremation grounds, nor land frequented by sinners.
One who places rice-balls for ancestors on another's land: by the owner's ancestors that funeral rite is destroyed.
Therefore the wise should buy land and give it, even a little; the rice-ball given to ancestors on it is everlasting.
Forests, mountains, rivers, sacred fords and lakes they say are ownerless, for there is no possession.
Thus the fruit of the gift of land has been told, lord of men; now I shall tell you of the gift of cows, sinless one.
Cows are above ascetics and all others; therefore the god Maheshvara took up austerity with them.
They live in Brahma's world with Soma, Bharata; Brahmarishis and Siddhas seek the supreme goal through them.
They help with milk, offering, curds, dung, hide, bones, horns and hair, Bharata.
For them there is never cold or heat, as they always do their work; no rain, nor trouble, nor sorrow befalls them.
They go with brahmanas; therefore the wise say cows and brahmanas are one, a higher state.
They were made animals for the god's sacrifice; then the river Charmanvati, king, arose from cow-hides.
Freed from animalhood, they were made for giving; whoever, lord of the earth, gives these to the chief of brahmanas crosses a hard calamity, even in rough circumstances, king.
The giver of a thousand cows does not see hell after death and gains victory everywhere, lord of men.
The lord of gods said that cow's milk is nectar; therefore he who gives a cow gives nectar.
Knowers of the Veda know it as the imperishable offering of the fires; therefore he who gives a cow gives an offering.
This is heaven embodied: one who gives a bull, lord of cows, to a brahmana of qualities is honoured in heaven.
These are called the breaths of living beings, bull of the Bharatas; therefore he who gives a cow gives breaths.
Knowers of the Veda know cows to be the refuge of beings; therefore he who gives a cow gives refuge.
A cow should not be given for killing, nor to a miser, nor a non-believer, nor to one who lives by cows, bull among men.
A man who gives cows to such sinful people goes to imperishable hell, so say the wise.
One should not give a cow to a brahmana that is lean, with a bad calf, barren, diseased, deformed or exhausted.
The giver of ten thousand cows rejoices rightly with Shakra; a man who gives a hundred thousand gains imperishable worlds.
Thus the gift of cows, the gift of sesame and the gift of land have been told; now hear of food, Bharata.
The gift of food is called the chief, Kaunteya; by giving food Rantideva went to heaven; he sees the greatly fortunate Svayambhuva, lord of men.
Not by gold, garments or the gift of a horse, Bharata, do men gain the good as those who give food here, lord.
Food is the highest wealth, and Shri is held greater; from food breath arises, and splendour, vigour and strength.
The man who always gives food to the good with one-pointed mind does not meet hard places: so said Parashara.
Having honoured by rule, one should offer food to the gods; the king whose food a man eats, his gods eat the same.
Whoever makes a gift of food on the Kaumudi day in the bright fortnight,
crosses hard places and gains endlessness after death.
One who, composed, gives food to a guest without eating first, bull of the Bharatas, gains the worlds of the knowers of Brahman.
A giver of food who has fallen into a very hard calamity crosses it; he crosses sin here and draws off misdeed.
Thus the fruit of the gifts of food, sesame, land and cows has been told.
[Yudhishthira said:] The gift of drinking water is the highest; how is it of great fruit here? I wish to hear this at length, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] Come, I shall tell you duly, bull of the Bharatas; hear from me as I tell, truth-valiant one, I shall tell you everything beginning with the gift of drinking water, sinless one.
Having given food and drink, a man gains; there is no gift higher than that, I think.
From food, dear one, all breathing beings proceed; therefore food is called the highest of all gifts in the world.
From food strength and splendour of beings always grow; therefore the Prajapati called the gift of food the best.
You have heard Savitri's good words too, Kaunteya, whence this is and how, great-minded one, in the sacrifice of the gods.
When food is given by a man here, breaths are given; and there is here no higher gift than the gift of life.
You have heard, mighty-armed, Lomasha's word about what Shibi formerly gained by giving his life to a dove.
He gains all desires and everlasting fame here, and after death endlessness, and is freed from sins.
The giver of water, tiger among men, going to heaven gains imperishable worlds, so Manu said.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of a brahmana and Yama, Yudhishthira.
In the middle country there was a great village of brahmanas, between the Ganga and Yamuna, below the Yamuna mountain.
Famed as Parnashala, lovely, king; many learned brahmanas then lived there.
Then Yama said to a certain man in black garments, red-eyed, with raised hair, crow-shanked, with nose and eyes of a crow:

Go, brahmana, to the village and bring Agastya from there, by gotra and by name, Sharmin.
mahabharata:13:67.7	Learned, set in peace, a teacher, unhonoured; and do not bring any other, who is of his gotra at his side.
mahabharata:13:67.8	For he has such qualities, equal in study and birth, in offspring and in conduct, with the whole of the wise one; bring him as pointed out; honour is to be done to him by me.
Going, he did the opposite of Yama's command; seizing him who had been forbidden by Yama, he brought him.
Sesame should be eaten, and anointing with it should always be done by those wishing good, in the house, with their whole selves.
Water should be always given and drunk, without doubt; one should dig ponds, tanks and wells here.
This is very hard to get in the world, best of the twice-born; water should always be given by you; this is unsurpassed merit.
Water-sheds should be made for drinking by you constantly, best of the twice-born; and after eating, drinking water especially is to be given.
Thus told by that messenger of Yama, he was taken home and did all that command of Yama.
The messenger of Yama, having brought and taken Sharmin, went and reported him to the King of Dharma.
The mighty King of Dharma, honouring that knower of dharma, made an agreement with him and sent him away as he came.
Yama gave him all instruction too, and returning, he did all that Yama had said.
Yama likewise praises lamps, wishing the good of the ancestors; therefore the giver of lamps constantly carries the ancestors across.
Lamps should be given constantly, best of the Bharatas; they are held to be the eye of gods and ancestors, lord.
The gift of jewels is said to be of great merit, lord of men; a brahmana who sells them and sacrifices gives safety.
What a brahmana, having received, gives to brahmanas is imperishable for both giver and receiver.
He who gives, standing in his station, a gift to one such, the dharma of both is imperishable; so said Manu, knower of dharma.
By giving garments a man devoted to his own wives becomes well clothed and well dressed, so we have heard.
Cows, gold and sesame have been described many times, tiger among men, by seeing the authority of the Veda.
One should marry and beget sons; the gain of a son, Kauravya, is more distinguished than every gain.
[Yudhishthira said:] A kshatriya may give the earth; a brahmana should duly accept it by his own deed; no other deserves to give.
What can be given by all classes by those wishing fruit, or what is declared in the Veda, you ought to tell me.
[Bhishma said:] Three things of equal name and equal fruit are to be given, with fruit of all desires: cows, earth and learning.
One who also tells his pupil the righteous Brahmic Sarasvati gains fruit equal to that of the gift of earth and cows.
So they praise cows, and nothing higher is to be given than them; their fruit is near and their cost light, Yudhishthira; cows are mothers of all beings, giving all comfort.
Cows are to be circumambulated by those who wish prosperity, constantly; the goddesses are the house of auspiciousness; therefore they are always to be honoured.
Let the instruction made by the gods go on in the works of cows; only the former syllable is to be said, nothing else in any way.
At pasture or at a watering-place the wise should not trouble cows; thirsty and looking, they would strike a man with his kinsmen.
Whatever dharma he performs, and whatever the fruit of its merit, he who gives a share of all, by that all engagements go on.
He who begets him, he who saves him from fear, and he who makes his livelihood: all these are three fathers.
Service to the teacher destroys stain, pride destroys great fame, three sons remove childlessness, and ten cows remove lack of livelihood.
To one devoted to the Vedanta, of much learning, content in wisdom, master of his senses, good, self-controlled and restrained, and always speaking kindly to beings,
who does no wrong from fear of hunger, gentle, self-controlled and always hospitable, to a brahmana of equal conduct with sons and wife one should assign a livelihood.

As great as is the merit in giving a cow to a good vessel, so great is the fault in taking a brahmana's property; in all states the taking of a brahmana's property, and their wives, are to be avoided from afar.
[Bhishma said:] When Dvaravati was being settled long ago, Partha, so we have heard, a great well was seen, covered with grass and creepers.
Making effort there, those seeking water from that well, joined with great toil, in the water that was covered,
saw a huge lizard staying there; and they made effort by thousands to lift it.
Binding that mountain-like creature with ropes and leather straps, they could not lift it, and went to Janardana.
A great lizard stands covering the mouth of the well; there is none to lift it: so they reported to Krishna.
Lifted by Vasudeva and asked what he wished, King Nriga then told himself, the ancient sacrificer of a thousand sacrifices.
As he spoke so, Madhava said to him: "Good deeds were done by you, no sin; how did you come to such an ill state, king? Tell me what this is."
We have heard here that you gave earlier a hundred thousand cows, again hundreds, eight hundreds, and tens of thousands to the twice-born, king; where has that gone?

I begged the receiver by exchange of a hundred times a hundred cows, but he said this to me:
mahabharata:13:69.15	'A cow suited to place and time, patient, not calf-loving, giver of sweet milk, blessed, is always in my house.
mahabharata:13:69.16	The cow that nourishes my lean son without breast I cannot give up,' and he went.
mahabharata:13:69.17	Then I begged another brahmana by exchange: 'Take a hundred thousand cows for that one.'
mahabharata:13:69.18	[The brahmana said:] 'I do not accept from kings; I am able in seeking my own; let that very cow be given quickly to me, Madhusudana.'
mahabharata:13:69.19	Though I offered gold, horses, silver and chariots, that bull among brahmanas did not accept and went.
mahabharata:13:69.20	At this very time, urged by the law of time, I reached the world of the ancestors and came to the King of Dharma.
mahabharata:13:69.21	Yama, honouring me, then said: 'No end is counted of your merit, king.
mahabharata:13:69.22	But a sin was done by you through ignorance; practise it first or afterward, as you wish.'
mahabharata:13:69.23	'You said I protect"; your promise was untrue; and taking a brahmana's property: yours is a threefold transgression.'
'First I shall bear the hardship and afterward the good': saying so to the King of Dharma, I fell on the ground.
I heard as I fell Yama speaking loudly: 'Vasudeva Janardana will be your lifter.
When a thousand years are complete and the evil deed is exhausted, you will gain eternal worlds won by your own deed.'
I saw myself fallen head-down in the well and having reached an animal womb, but memory did not leave me.
I have been carried across by you today; what else is there except the power of austerity? Give me leave, Krishna; let me go to heaven today."
Permitted by Krishna, bowing to Janardana, he mounted a divine car and went to heaven, scourge of foes.
When Nriga had gone to heaven, best of the Bharatas, Vasudeva sang this verse, descendant of the Kurus:

A brahmana's property must not be taken by a man who knows; a brahmana's property taken kills, as a brahmin cow killed Nriga.
mahabharata:13:69.32	Meeting with the good among the good is not fruitless, Partha; see Nriga freed from hell by meeting with the good.
mahabharata:13:69.33	The gift there had fruit, and the malice there had none; therefore, Yudhishthira, one should avoid wrong to cows.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the words of the sage Uddalaki and of Nachiketas, both.
The sage Uddalaki, having undertaken a vow, said to his son Nachiketas, "Serve me"; and when the observance was complete, the great sage said to his son:
Attached to ablutions and intent on study, fuel, kusha grass, flowers, a water-pot and water on all sides were forgotten by me; take them and come here from the river bank.
Going and not finding all that, swept by the river's current, "I do not see it," the sage said to his father.
Possessed by hunger, thirst and fatigue, the sage Uddalaki then cursed his son, saying "See Yama," that great ascetic.
Thus struck by his father with a thunderbolt of words, with joined palms he said "Be gracious" and fell to the ground, his life gone.
Seeing Nachiketas fallen, his father, fainting with sorrow, said "What have I done?" and fell on the ground.
Embracing his own son, afflicted with sorrow, the rest of that day passed for him, and the fierce night.
Son, have you won good worlds by your own deed? By good fortune you are back; your body is not human.
The seer of all, asked by his great-souled father, told him the truth in the midst of the great sages.

Doing your command, I quickly went and, reaching the vast, lovely, splendid assembly hall of Vaivasvata, I saw it, made of gold and earth for thousands of yojanas.
mahabharata:13:70.15	Seeing me come toward him, Vaivasvata gave a seat in the house and honoured me for your sake with guest-water and other honours.
mahabharata:13:70.16	Then I said to him slowly, as he was honoured, surrounded by assembly members: 'I have come to your domain, king of dharma; assign to me the worlds I deserve.'
How should I behave toward him, how not be abandoned by him? Rejected by him too, I do not wish to live.
[Vaishampayana said:] Thus addressed by Vyasa of wonderful deeds, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, of great splendour, replied.
Seeing Dvaraka and those women of Krishna, Partha, weeping with sound, fell on the ground.
Dhrishtaketu, Jayatsena, King Satyajit, Duryodhana's sons and Shakuni Saubala,
